title: Permutations and Combinations
subtitle: Quantitative Aptitude – Placement Preparation
description: Learn fundamental counting principles, factorials, permutations, combinations, arrangements with restrictions, circular permutations, repeated objects, selections and distribution methods commonly tested in placement examinations.
learningObjectives: Understand the fundamental principle of counting.
Understand factorial notation and its properties.
Calculate arrangements using the permutation formula.
Calculate selections using the combination formula.
Handle restrictions such as objects being together or separated.
Arrange vowels, consonants, digits and letters under given conditions.
Form numbers using given digits with and without repetition.
Select committees and teams under different conditions.
Use complementary counting for selection problems.
Use placement-test shortcuts to solve counting questions quickly.

sections.heading: 1. Fundamental Principle of Counting
content: The fundamental principle of counting helps determine the total number of outcomes when a task is completed through multiple stages.
If one operation can be performed in m ways and another independent operation can be performed in n ways, both operations together can be performed in m × n ways.
The multiplication principle is used when all stages must be completed.
The addition principle is used when exactly one among mutually exclusive alternatives must be chosen.
formulas: Total ways for successive independent stages = m × n × p × ...
Total ways for mutually exclusive alternatives = m + n + p + ...

examples.question: A student has 4 shirts and 3 trousers. In how many ways can the student choose one shirt and one trouser?
examples.solution: For each of the 4 shirts, any of the 3 trousers can be selected. Total ways = 4 × 3 = 12.

examples.question: A person can travel from City A to City B by 3 buses or 2 trains. In how many ways can the person travel?
examples.solution: The person chooses either a bus or a train. Total ways = 3 + 2 = 5.

sections.heading: 2. Factorials
content: The factorial of a positive integer n is the product of all positive integers from 1 to n.
Factorials are extensively used in permutations and combinations.
By definition, 0 factorial and 1 factorial are both equal to 1.
Factorial expressions can often be simplified by cancelling common factors.

examples.question: Find the value of 6!.
Simplify 10!/8!.

sections.heading: 3. Permutations
content: A permutation is an arrangement of objects in a specific order.
In permutation problems, changing the order creates a different arrangement.
The number of ways to arrange r objects selected from n distinct objects is written as nPr.
Use permutations when positions, ranks or order are important.
formulas: nPr = n!/(n − r)!
nPn = n!
nP1 = n

examples.question: In how many ways can 3 students be arranged from a group of 5 students?
examples.solution: The order matters. Therefore, 5P3 = 5!/(5 − 3)! = 5!/2! = 5 × 4 × 3 = 60.

examples.question: In how many ways can 6 different books be arranged on a shelf?
examples.solution: All 6 books are arranged. Total arrangements = 6! = 720.

sections.heading: 4. Combinations
content: A combination is a selection of objects without considering their order.
In combination problems, changing the order does not create a new selection.
The number of ways to select r objects from n distinct objects is written as nCr.
Use combinations when forming groups, teams, committees or selections.
formulas: nCr = n!/[r!(n − r)!]
nC0 = 1
nCn = 1
nC1 = n

examples.question: In how many ways can 3 students be selected from 5 students?
examples.solution: The order does not matter. Therefore, 5C3 = 5!/(3! × 2!) = 10.

examples.question: In how many ways can a committee of 2 people be selected from 6 people?
examples.solution: Number of committees = 6C2 = 6 × 5/2 = 15.

sections.heading: 5. Difference Between Permutation and Combination
content: Permutation refers to arrangement, while combination refers to selection.
Order matters in permutations but does not matter in combinations.
Words such as arrange, rank, seat, code and number generally indicate permutations.
Words such as choose, select, committee, group and team generally indicate combinations.
formulas: nPr = nCr × r!
nCr = nPr/r!

examples.question: Three students are selected from 7 students and assigned the roles of captain, vice-captain and secretary. How many possibilities are there?
examples.solution: The roles are different, so order matters. Total possibilities = 7P3 = 7 × 6 × 5 = 210.

examples.question: Three students are selected from 7 students to form a committee. How many committees are possible?
examples.solution: There are no separate roles, so order does not matter. Total committees = 7C3 = 35.

sections.heading: 6. Important Properties of Combinations
content: Selecting r objects is equivalent to rejecting n − r objects.
This symmetry can simplify calculations involving large values of r.
The sum of all possible combinations of n objects is 2^n.
The sum excluding the empty selection is 2^n − 1.
formulas: nCr = nC(n − r)
nCr + nC(r − 1) = (n + 1)Cr
nC0 + nC1 + ... + nCn = 2^n

examples.question: Find 10C8.
How many non-empty groups can be formed from 5 people?
examples.solution: Each person can either be selected or not selected. Total non-empty groups = 2^5 − 1 = 31.

sections.heading: 7. Arranging All Distinct Objects
content: The number of ways to arrange n distinct objects in a row is n factorial.
Each position is filled successively using the multiplication principle.
This method applies to distinct people, letters, books and other unique objects.
formulas: Linear arrangements of n distinct objects = n!

examples.question: In how many ways can the letters of the word MATH be arranged?
examples.solution: All 4 letters are distinct. Number of arrangements = 4! = 24.

examples.question: In how many ways can 7 people stand in a line?
examples.solution: Number of arrangements = 7! = 5040.

sections.heading: 8. Arrangements with Repeated Objects
content: When some objects are identical, interchanging identical objects does not create a new arrangement.
Divide the factorial of the total number of objects by the factorial of each repetition count.
This method is commonly used for arranging letters of words containing repeated letters.
formulas: Arrangements of n objects where p, q, r, ... objects are identical = n!/(p!q!r!...)

examples.question: How many distinct arrangements can be formed using the letters of LEVEL?
examples.solution: LEVEL has 5 letters, with L repeated twice and E repeated twice. Arrangements = 5!/(2! × 2!) = 30.

examples.question: How many distinct arrangements are possible for the word BANANA?
examples.solution: BANANA has 6 letters, with A repeated 3 times and N repeated 2 times. Arrangements = 6!/(3! × 2!) = 60.

sections.heading: 9. Objects That Must Always Be Together
content: When certain objects must remain together, treat them as a single block.
Arrange the block with the remaining objects.
Then multiply by the internal arrangements of the objects within the block.
This method is commonly called the block method.
formulas: Total arrangements = Arrangements of blocks × Internal arrangements

examples.question: In how many ways can 5 people stand in a row if A and B must stand together?
examples.solution: Treat A and B as one block. There are now 4 units, which can be arranged in 4! ways. A and B can switch places in 2! ways. Total = 4! × 2! = 48.

examples.question: How many arrangements of the word SCHOOL have all vowels together?
examples.solution: The vowels O and O form one block. The units are the vowel block, S, C, H and L, giving 5 units. Since the two O's are identical, internal arrangements equal 1. Total = 5! = 120.

sections.heading: 10. Objects That Must Not Be Together
content: Use complementary counting when particular objects must not be together.
First calculate all unrestricted arrangements.
Then subtract the arrangements in which the restricted objects are together.
This is usually faster than directly counting separated arrangements.
formulas: Required arrangements = Total arrangements − Restricted arrangements

examples.question: In how many ways can 5 people stand in a row if A and B must not stand together?
examples.solution: Total arrangements = 5! = 120. Arrangements with A and B together = 4! × 2! = 48. Required arrangements = 120 − 48 = 72.

examples.question: In how many ways can the letters of MANGO be arranged if M and A are not together?
examples.solution: Total arrangements = 5! = 120. Arrangements with M and A together = 4! × 2! = 48. Required arrangements = 72.

sections.heading: 11. Arrangements with No Two Similar Objects Together
content: First arrange the objects of one category.
Count the gaps created before, between and after those objects.
Place the objects of the other category into the available gaps.
This method is commonly used when vowels or particular people must not be adjacent.
formulas: If n objects are arranged, they create n + 1 gaps
Choose required gaps and arrange the remaining objects

examples.question: In how many ways can 3 boys and 2 girls stand in a row if no two girls stand together?
examples.solution: Arrange the 3 boys in 3! ways. They create 4 gaps. Select 2 of the 4 gaps and arrange the girls: 4C2 × 2!. Total = 3! × 4C2 × 2! = 72.

examples.question: In how many ways can 4 men and 3 women stand in a row if no two women stand together?
examples.solution: Arrange the men in 4! ways. They create 5 gaps. Choose 3 gaps and arrange the women. Total = 4! × 5C3 × 3! = 1440.

sections.heading: 12. Vowels and Consonants
content: Separate the vowels and consonants before applying restrictions.
For vowels together, treat all vowels as one block.
For vowels occupying only specified positions, first choose or identify those positions.
Account for repeated letters when necessary.
formulas: Vowels together = Arrange the vowel block and consonants × Arrange vowels internally
Vowels in selected positions = Choose positions × Arrange vowels × Arrange consonants

examples.question: In how many ways can the letters of MOBILE be arranged if all vowels are together?
examples.solution: The vowels O, I and E form one block. Along with M, B and L, there are 4 units. Arrange the units in 4! ways and vowels internally in 3! ways. Total = 4! × 3! = 144.

examples.question: In how many ways can the letters of EQUATION be arranged so that all vowels are together?
examples.solution: EQUATION has 5 distinct vowels and 3 distinct consonants. Treat the vowels as one block, giving 4 units. Total arrangements = 4! × 5! = 2880.

sections.heading: 13. Forming Numbers Without Repetition
content: When forming numbers, the first digit cannot be zero.
Fill the first position separately when zero is among the available digits.
After selecting the first digit, fill the remaining positions using permutations.
Without repetition, a digit cannot be used more than once.
formulas: r-digit numbers from n non-zero distinct digits without repetition = nPr
When zero is included, handle the first digit separately

examples.question: How many 3-digit numbers can be formed from 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 without repetition?
examples.solution: The number of arrangements is 5P3 = 5 × 4 × 3 = 60.

examples.question: How many 3-digit numbers can be formed from 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4 without repetition?
examples.solution: The first digit has 4 choices because it cannot be zero. The second digit then has 4 choices and the third has 3 choices. Total = 4 × 4 × 3 = 48.

sections.heading: 14. Forming Numbers with Repetition
content: When repetition is allowed, a selected digit may be used again.
Each position generally has the same number of choices unless the first position cannot contain zero.
Use the multiplication principle to calculate the total.
formulas: r-digit strings from n digits with repetition = n^r
r-digit numbers using 0 to n − 1 = (n − 1) × n^(r − 1)

examples.question: How many 4-digit codes can be formed using digits 1 to 6 when repetition is allowed?
examples.solution: Each of the 4 positions has 6 choices. Total codes = 6^4 = 1296.

examples.question: How many 3-digit numbers can be formed using digits 0 to 5 when repetition is allowed?
examples.solution: The first digit has 5 choices, excluding zero. Each remaining digit has 6 choices. Total = 5 × 6 × 6 = 180.

sections.heading: 15. Numbers with Divisibility Conditions
content: Use divisibility rules to restrict the possible final digits or digit groups.
For an even number, the final digit must be even.
For a number divisible by 5, the final digit must be 0 or 5.
After selecting the restricted digit, arrange the remaining digits.
formulas: Even number: Last digit must be 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8
Divisible by 5: Last digit must be 0 or 5

examples.question: How many 3-digit even numbers can be formed using 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 without repetition?
examples.solution: The final digit must be 2 or 4, giving 2 choices. The first digit then has 4 choices and the middle digit has 3 choices. Total = 2 × 4 × 3 = 24.

examples.question: How many 4-digit numbers divisible by 5 can be formed using 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 without repetition?
examples.solution: The final digit must be 5 because zero is unavailable. The remaining three positions can be filled from the other 5 digits in 5P3 ways. Total = 5 × 4 × 3 = 60.

sections.heading: 16. Circular Permutations
content: In a circular arrangement, rotations are considered identical.
Fix one object and arrange the remaining objects around it.
For people seated around a round table, the number of arrangements is (n − 1)!.
When clockwise and anticlockwise arrangements are also considered identical, divide by 2.
formulas: Circular arrangements of n distinct objects = (n − 1)!
Circular arrangements when clockwise and anticlockwise orders are identical = (n − 1)!/2

examples.question: In how many ways can 6 people sit around a circular table?
examples.solution: Circular arrangements = (6 − 1)! = 5! = 120.

examples.question: In how many ways can 8 distinct beads be arranged in a necklace?
examples.solution: For a necklace, clockwise and anticlockwise arrangements are identical. Total = (8 − 1)!/2 = 7!/2 = 2520.

sections.heading: 17. Circular Arrangements with Restrictions
content: For adjacent people, treat them as one block before applying circular arrangements.
For people who must not sit together, subtract adjacent arrangements from total circular arrangements.
Fix one person to remove rotational duplication.
Carefully distinguish between round-table and necklace arrangements.
formulas: Two particular people together around a circle = 2 × (n − 2)!
Two particular people not together = (n − 1)! − 2 × (n − 2)!

examples.question: In how many ways can 6 people sit around a table if A and B must sit together?
examples.solution: Treat A and B as one block. There are 5 circular units, arranged in (5 − 1)! ways. A and B can switch positions in 2 ways. Total = 4! × 2 = 48.

examples.question: In how many ways can 6 people sit around a table if A and B must not sit together?
examples.solution: Total arrangements = 5! = 120. Arrangements with A and B together = 48. Required arrangements = 120 − 48 = 72.

sections.heading: 18. Committee and Team Selection
content: Committee formation is generally a combination because order does not matter.
When particular members must be included, select them first and choose the remaining members.
When particular members must be excluded, remove them from the available group.
For conditions such as at least or at most, divide the problem into valid cases.
formulas: Committee of r from n people = nCr
If k particular people must be included = (n − k)C(r − k)
If k particular people are excluded = (n − k)Cr

examples.question: In how many ways can a committee of 4 be formed from 8 people?
examples.solution: Number of committees = 8C4 = 70.

examples.question: In how many ways can a committee of 4 be formed from 8 people if A must be included?
examples.solution: Include A and select the remaining 3 members from the other 7 people. Total = 7C3 = 35.

sections.heading: 19. Selection with Men and Women
content: Split the selection according to the required number of men and women.
Calculate each valid case using combinations.
Add the results of mutually exclusive valid cases.
For at least one person from a category, complementary counting is often faster.
formulas: Select x men and y women = mCx × wCy
At least one woman = Total selections − Selections containing no women

examples.question: A committee of 3 is selected from 5 men and 4 women. In how many ways can it contain exactly 2 men and 1 woman?
examples.solution: Select 2 men from 5 and 1 woman from 4. Total = 5C2 × 4C1 = 10 × 4 = 40.

examples.question: A team of 4 is selected from 6 men and 3 women. In how many ways can it contain at least one woman?
examples.solution: Total teams = 9C4 = 126. Teams with no women = 6C4 = 15. Required teams = 126 − 15 = 111.

sections.heading: 20. At Least and At Most Conditions
content: At least means the stated number or more.
At most means the stated number or fewer.
List all valid cases and add their counts.
Use the complement when the excluded cases are easier to calculate.
formulas: At least one = Total − None
At most r = Sum of cases from 0 through r

examples.question: A committee of 4 is selected from 5 men and 3 women. In how many ways can it contain at least 2 women?
examples.solution: Valid cases are 2 women and 2 men, or 3 women and 1 man. Total = 3C2 × 5C2 + 3C3 × 5C1 = 3 × 10 + 1 × 5 = 35.

examples.question: From 6 men and 4 women, how many groups of 3 contain at most one woman?
examples.solution: Valid cases are no women or exactly one woman. Total = 6C3 + 4C1 × 6C2 = 20 + 4 × 15 = 80.

sections.heading: 21. Selection of Particular Objects
content: When some specified objects must be selected, include them first.
When specified objects must not be selected, remove them from the available objects.
When exactly one among specified objects must be selected, form separate cases.
When two objects cannot be selected together, subtract selections containing both.
formulas: Both A and B included in an r-member group = (n − 2)C(r − 2)
Neither A nor B included = (n − 2)Cr
A and B not together in selection = nCr − (n − 2)C(r − 2)

examples.question: In how many ways can 4 students be selected from 9 students if A and B must both be selected?
examples.solution: Select A and B first. Choose the remaining 2 students from the other 7. Total = 7C2 = 21.

examples.question: In how many ways can 4 students be selected from 9 students if A and B cannot both be selected?
examples.solution: Total selections = 9C4 = 126. Selections containing both A and B = 7C2 = 21. Required selections = 126 − 21 = 105.

sections.heading: 22. Distribution of Distinct Objects
content: When distinct objects are distributed to distinct people, each object may independently be assigned to one of the people.
If every person may receive any number of objects, including none, use the multiplication principle.
Additional restrictions require case analysis or inclusion-exclusion.
formulas: Distributing n distinct objects among r distinct people without restrictions = r^n

examples.question: In how many ways can 4 distinct books be distributed among 3 students if a student may receive any number of books?
examples.solution: Each of the 4 books has 3 possible recipients. Total distributions = 3^4 = 81.

examples.question: In how many ways can 5 different prizes be awarded to 4 students if a student can receive more than one prize?
examples.solution: Each prize has 4 possible recipients. Total ways = 4^5 = 1024.

sections.heading: 23. Distribution of Identical Objects
content: Identical-object distribution commonly uses the stars-and-bars method.
For non-negative distributions, a recipient may receive zero objects.
For positive distributions, every recipient must receive at least one object.
Convert minimum-allocation conditions by giving the required minimum first.
formulas: Distribute n identical objects among r people, allowing zero = (n + r − 1)C(r − 1)
Distribute n identical objects among r people, each receiving at least one = (n − 1)C(r − 1)

examples.question: In how many ways can 7 identical chocolates be distributed among 3 children if a child may receive none?
examples.solution: Using stars and bars, the number of distributions is (7 + 3 − 1)C(3 − 1) = 9C2 = 36.

examples.question: In how many ways can 7 identical chocolates be distributed among 3 children if every child receives at least one?
examples.solution: Give one chocolate to each child first. The required count is (7 − 1)C(3 − 1) = 6C2 = 15.

sections.heading: 24. Placement-Test Strategy
content: First identify whether the question involves arrangement or selection.
Use permutations when order, position, rank or role matters.
Use combinations when only the selected group matters.
Apply the block method when objects must remain together.
Use total minus unwanted arrangements when objects must not be together.
Handle zero separately when forming numbers.
Use gap arrangements when similar objects must be separated.
Use complementary counting for at-least-one conditions.
Check whether repeated objects are identical.
For circular arrangements, fix one object before arranging the others.
Simplify factorial expressions before performing large multiplications.
Divide the problem into mutually exclusive cases when there are multiple conditions.
formulas: Permutation: nPr = n!/(n − r)!
Combination: nCr = n!/[r!(n − r)!]
Relation: nPr = nCr × r!
Repeated objects: n!/(p!q!r!...)
Circular permutation: (n − 1)!
At least one = Total − None

examples.question: From 8 employees, a manager and an assistant manager must be selected. In how many ways can this be done?
examples.solution: The two positions are different, so order matters. Total ways = 8P2 = 8 × 7 = 56.

examples.question: From 8 employees, two representatives must be selected. In how many ways can this be done?
examples.solution: The representatives have identical roles, so order does not matter. Total ways = 8C2 = 28.

quickShortcuts.title: Arrangement or selection
quickShortcuts.note: Use permutations for arrangements and combinations for selections.

quickShortcuts.title: Factorial expansion
quickShortcuts.note: Expand only enough terms to cancel the denominator.

quickShortcuts.title: Arrange all objects
quickShortcuts.note: The number of linear arrangements of n distinct objects is n!.

quickShortcuts.title: Permutation formula
quickShortcuts.note: Use nPr = n!/(n − r)! when order matters.

quickShortcuts.title: Combination formula
quickShortcuts.note: Use nCr = n!/[r!(n − r)!] when order does not matter.

quickShortcuts.title: Combination symmetry
quickShortcuts.note: Use nCr = nC(n − r) to reduce calculations.

quickShortcuts.title: Permutation-combination relation
quickShortcuts.note: nPr = nCr × r!.

quickShortcuts.title: Repeated letters
quickShortcuts.note: Divide total factorial by the factorial of each repetition count.

quickShortcuts.title: Always together
quickShortcuts.note: Treat the required objects as one block.

quickShortcuts.title: Never together
quickShortcuts.note: Subtract together-arrangements from total arrangements.

quickShortcuts.title: No two together
quickShortcuts.note: Arrange one category first and place the other category in gaps.

quickShortcuts.title: Circular arrangement
quickShortcuts.note: For n distinct people around a table, use (n − 1)!.

quickShortcuts.title: Necklace arrangement
quickShortcuts.note: Use (n − 1)!/2 when clockwise and anticlockwise arrangements are identical.

quickShortcuts.title: Number formation
quickShortcuts.note: Zero cannot occupy the first position of a number.

quickShortcuts.title: Even-number formation
quickShortcuts.note: Choose the final even digit first.

quickShortcuts.title: Divisibility by 5
quickShortcuts.note: Choose 0 or 5 as the final digit.

quickShortcuts.title: Particular person included
quickShortcuts.note: Fix that person and select the remaining members.

quickShortcuts.title: At least one
quickShortcuts.note: Use total selections minus selections containing none.

quickShortcuts.title: Non-empty subsets
quickShortcuts.note: A set with n elements has 2^n − 1 non-empty subsets.

quickShortcuts.title: Distinct-object distribution
quickShortcuts.note: n distinct objects distributed among r people gives r^n unrestricted assignments.

commonMistakes: Using permutations when only selection is required.
Using combinations when roles or positions are different.
Forgetting that order matters in passwords, rankings and seat arrangements.
Treating repeated objects as distinct.
Failing to divide by factorials of repeated letters.
Forgetting internal arrangements when using the block method.
Subtracting the wrong restricted case in not-together problems.
Using n! instead of (n − 1)! for circular arrangements.
Dividing round-table arrangements by 2 unnecessarily.
Forgetting to divide necklace arrangements by 2.
Allowing zero in the first position while forming a number.
Forgetting to restrict the last digit in even-number problems.
Using addition instead of multiplication for successive choices.
Using multiplication instead of addition for mutually exclusive cases.
Not considering every valid case in at-least or at-most questions.
Counting overlapping cases more than once.
Forgetting to include compulsory members before selecting the others.
Applying nCr = nC(n − r) incorrectly.
Calculating large factorials without first cancelling common factors.
Confusing identical-object distribution with distinct-object distribution.
